title: Beyond the claim: Why lab stewardship has become essential for health plans
summary: Electronic health records integrations with genetic testing increases operational efficiency, enhances the provider experience and offers precision medicine at scale.
body_markdown:
Laboratory stewardship has evolved well beyond the traditional goal of reducing unnecessary testing. For health plans, many of the most persistent reimbursement challenges don't begin at claim adjudication.


They begin much earlier, at the point a test is ordered. Documentation gaps, nonspecific coding, misalignment around medical necessity, and inappropriate utilization all originate upstream, long before a claim is submitted, yet they often surface downstream as denials, payment delays, administrative burden and associated costs for both providers and health plans alike.


That’s why lab stewardship has become a critical strategy for health plans. Rather than focusing solely on reducing unnecessary testing, stewardship addresses problems across the entire testing life cycle. It strengthens the clinical and administrative foundations that support accurate reimbursement, quality care, and better patient outcomes.


### For payers, providers, and labs, stewardship now centers on:


- Improving the test selection process to drive the right test at the right time for the right patient
- Supporting more complete clinical information at the point of laboratory ordering
- Encouraging appropriate utilization (reducing duplicate testing)
- Working with plans to find and close[gaps in care](https://www.labcorp.com/organizations/capabilities/quality-performance/gaps-in-care)


As healthcare organizations continue to balance quality, affordability, member experience, and regulatory requirements, lab stewardship offers a practical framework for aligning clinical intent with payer expectations. At its core, lab stewardship is about making sure the right patient receives the right test at the right time while minimizing avoidable administrative burdens and financial concerns.


For health plans, every lab order that enters the system carries with it a cascade of administrative, clinical, and financial impacts. When that cascade is well managed, care improves. When it isn't, friction builds in the form of:


- Denied claims
- Miscoded members
- Undertested populations
- Higher patient out-of-pocket costs
- Missed opportunities to intervene before a condition becomes a crisis


Lab stewardship is the discipline that decreases the amount of friction. And increasingly, health plans that take lab stewardship seriously are discovering it reaches far deeper into their operations than initially expected.


## How Labcorp defines lab stewardship


The term lab stewardship has historically lived inside clinical walls, associated with reducing unnecessary testing and lowering costs. Lab stewardship is the coordinated effort to make sure every lab test ordered is appropriate, high-value and acted upon, so members get the right test at the right time. It reduces low-value and duplicative testing, guides clinicians toward evidence-based choices, closes gaps in care, and uses data to show the impact. The result is better outcomes for members and lower avoidable spend for the plan. But as healthcare has become more interconnected, data-driven, and financially complex, a broader and more practical definition has emerged.


Today's testing environment extends far beyond the lab itself. A single order can influence diagnostic decisions, care management strategies, quality performance measures, risk adjustment accuracy, reimbursement outcomes, and the member experience. Lab stewardship is not only about reducing unnecessary testing, now it focuses on ensuring patients receive the medically necessary testing needed, improving outcomes and thereby reducing medical spend.


For health plans, one of the greatest opportunities in laboratory stewardship lies in addressing both sides of overutilization. Unnecessary or duplicative testing can increase costs without improving care. Equally important, gaps in medically recommended testing can delay diagnosis, limit chronic disease monitoring, and prevent health plans from identifying members who may benefit from earlier intervention. A comprehensive stewardship strategy must address both challenges.


It must address how testing moves through the entire care and reimbursement ecosystem, from the initial clinical question to the final financial outcome. As a result, organizations are looking at deploying strategies that are designed to improve five core elements:


- Access to testing
- Test ordering
- Result retrieval
- Result interpretation
- Financial fairness


Each element affects whether clinical intent successfully translates into appropriate care, accurate documentation, proper coding, and efficient reimbursement. A breakdown at any point in the process can create obstacles that surface later as delayed diagnoses, extra administrative work, denied claims, unnecessary costs, or member dissatisfaction.


For payers, this broader definition reframes the conversation. Lab stewardship is more than a cost-control mechanism.


It's a framework for coordination that aligns labs, providers, and health plans around the shared goals of:


- Improving member outcomes
- Appropriate utilization
- Reducing administrative burden
- Creating more sustainable financial performance


## The payer reality check


As clinical evidence and standards of care evolve, policies may not always keep pace, creating gaps between recommended testing and covered services. Patients, providers, and payers frequently approach healthcare decisions with different expectations regarding how care should be utilized, delivered, and reimbursed.


Providers often view testing as part of the standard of care, but standards continue to evolve as new tests, treatments, and clinical evidence emerge. Payers evaluate coverage through a different lens that weighs:


- Clinical evidence standards
- Coverage policies and Medical necessity criteria
- Coding and documentation requirements
- Administrative rules, such as prior authorization
- Benefit design and pricing


These perspectives don’t inherently conflict, but disconnects arise when they aren’t aligned.[Researchers note](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34381860/) that aligning these perspectives remains difficult within a fragmented healthcare system.


That reality makes lab stewardship increasingly important. Effective stewardship translates clinical intent into workflows supporting both patient care and payer requirements.


Rather than assuming treatment automatically results in coverage, stewardship creates clearer connections between medical necessity, clinical documentation, and reimbursement expectations.


## The hidden problem in everyday claims


Most plan administrators are familiar with denial volumes, but few have mapped the precise reasons why they occur. Denials are often viewed as backend events, but the root causes frequently originate upstream, at test ordering, long before a claim reaches a payer.


According to[CMS criteria,](https://prismahealth.org/services/other-services/laboratory-services/laboratory-guidelines/denial-reasons) claims are commonly denied due to:


- Tests lacking documentation of medical necessity
- [Diagnostic codes](https://www.labcorp.com/how-lab-data-enables-more-accurate-patient-coding-value-based-care-success) submitted with a claim falling outside covered ICD-10 designations
- Testing frequency exceeding expected thresholds without supporting documentation
- A claim falling outside the[National Correct Coding Initiative](https://www.cms.gov/national-correct-coding-initiative-ncci) or[medically likely edits](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/national-correct-coding-initiative-ncci-edits/medicare-ncci-medically-unlikely-edits-mues) without demonstrated necessity


Medicare guidance specifically notes that failing to document medical necessity may result in denial, and claims submitted without appropriate diagnosis coding may face reimbursement challenges.


Coding specificity also matters. Generic coding can obscure clinically meaningful differences among tests, making it more difficult for payers to evaluate coverage eligibility and medical necessity.


None of these are laboratory errors per se. They are documentation and coding failures beginning at the point of care and work their way through the system until they surface as a denied claim or a delayed reimbursement. In many cases, denials are the predictable outcome of incomplete information submitted at the front end of the process.


Reimbursement starts with how a test is selected, described, documented, and coded, not simply how well it's performed. This is why medical-necessity alignment and coding specificity should be strategic priorities rather than purely administrative concerns. The claim is the final checkpoint in a process whose outcome was determined much earlier.


## Fixing it at the front end


Strong lab stewardship addresses these issues before claims are filed by promoting more transparent test selection practices, accurate documentation, and clearer diagnostic coding. The goal is to create greater front-end readiness so the clinical rationale supporting a test can be more easily understood, validated, and reimbursed when the claim reaches adjudication.


This is also where lab partners can play a more active role than many organizations realize. Modern stewardship programs are increasingly focused on helping providers capture the information necessary to support medical necessity at the time of ordering rather than attempting to resolve deficiencies after a denial occurs. By improving order quality upstream, plans can reduce downstream issues associated with rework, appeals, and reimbursement delays.


Labcorp's stewardship approach is designed on that principle. Tools such as eClaim Assist help providers improve order completeness and encourage accurate, more specific ICD-10 coding.


Stewardship resources and consultative support can also help strengthen documentation practices, align test selection with clinical indications, and create clearer connections between clinical intent and payer requirements. Rather than serving solely as a testing provider, Labcorp helps organizations address the documentation, coding, and medical-necessity gaps.


For payers, the value extends beyond claim outcomes. When documentation, coding, and test selection are aligned earlier in the process, claims become easier to adjudicate, medical necessity can be evaluated more efficiently, payers and providers experience less administrative burden, and members are less likely to encounter unexpected billing surprises.


Effective lab stewardship doesn't simply improve the performance of individual claims. It helps create a smoother, more transparent testing and reimbursement experience across the entire care continuum, reducing administrative expenses for payers and providers alike.


## The underutilization problem health plans often miss


When health plans focus on lab stewardship, the initial instinct is often to reduce unnecessary or duplicative tests that drive up costs. That focus on overutilization is reasonable but incomplete.


Underutilization is estimated to be[two to three times more common](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/three-lab-stewardship-utilization-rights-underutilization-focus) than overutilization. It creates risks such as:


- Delayed diagnoses
- Delayed treatment initiation
- Avoidable emergency department visits
- Increased healthcare costs


For plans with members managing chronic conditions, underutilization has direct financial implications as well. Patients with diabetes, cardiovascular concerns, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) who aren't well monitored tend to have increased emergency room visits and hospitalizations.


In fact, a study showed high-risk patients at an emergency department conducting higher rates of testing have[dramatically lower likelihood of adverse events as well as one-year mortality rates 34%](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9426758/) lower than high-risk patients seen at emergency departments with lower rates of diagnostic testing. Instead of increasing costs, earlier, more consistent and more appropriate testing redistributes costs toward earlier intervention and away from acute, high-cost episodes.


There is also a more immediate administrative dimension. Overly complex prior authorization processes designed to limit overutilization can inadvertently worsen underutilization. An[American Medical Association survey](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/exhausted-prior-auth-many-patients-abandon-care-ama-survey#:~:text=Most%20telling%20is%20that%2078,PDF)%20of%201%2C000%20practicing%20physicians.) found 78% of physicians believed the prior authorization process led patients to sometimes or often abandoning their recommended treatment, including ordered tests.


[Effective lab stewardship](https://www.labcorp.com/organizations/capabilities/lab-programs-partnerships/lab-stewardship) addresses both sides of the utilization equation by:


- Supporting real-time clinical decision-making
- Identifying and helping close gaps in care
- Reducing unnecessary duplication
- Giving clinicians access at point of care to relevant historical testing information when making diagnostic decisions


Lab stewardship isn’t about restricting access. It’s about aligning medically necessary care with payer requirements in ways that protect patients from unnecessary financial burdens while supporting better and more appropriate care.


## Coding accuracy as a population health lever


For plans operating in value-based care environments, coding accuracy is the foundation on which risk adjustment, quality performance, and shared savings calculations are built. Provider-assigned ICD-10 coding plays a key role in estimating expected healthcare costs. When coding is misaligned with clinical reality, providers and plans face an uphill battle meeting financial performance targets.


The gap between what laboratory data reveals and what gets coded can be significant. Working with large provider networks, Labcorp found coding for diabetes is generally well documented but still misses[20%-30% of patients](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/accurate-patient-coding-essential-improving-outcomes-and-value-based-care-performance-see-how-lab-1) .


CKD is more severely under-coded, with 70% or more of CKD patients uncoded or inaccurately staged. In[one analysis,](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/how-lab-data-enables-more-accurate-patient-coding-value-based-care-success) lab data identified 7,462 CKD patients, but only 2,105 had an associated ICD code on their most recent lab orders. Additionally, more than 50% of early-stage kidney disease patients lacked the urine test needed to accurately stage their condition.


For plans navigating CMS's V28 HCC model updates, which have nearly doubled CKD Risk Adjustment Factor (RAF) scores for several stages while reducing scores for some diabetes codes, these gaps carry real dollar consequences. Addressing uncoded and miscoded diabetes and CKD patients within a single ACO analysis projected a net[impact of nearly $14 million annually.](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/how-lab-data-enables-more-accurate-patient-coding-value-based-care-success)


## Building the infrastructure for better lab stewardship


The case for lab stewardship is clear. The harder question is how health plans and their lab partners build the infrastructure to act on it consistently.


Effective programs share five elements:


1. A clear vision with organizational alignment


2. The right skills for execution and management


3. Adequate resources


4. Incentives that motivate participation


5. A plan of action with defined metrics


Labcorp put this infrastructure into action with[one health system](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/driving-smarter-cardiac-testing-through-lab-stewardship) to replace unnecessary creatine kinase myocardial band (CK-MB) blood tests with the more appropriate troponin test through data-driven lab stewardship and order entry optimization. **The collaboration produced significant improvements:**


- 92% reduction in unnecessary CK-MB testing within one year
- Physicians gained confidence using troponin as the primary and standard test for suspected heart attacks
- Cardiac diagnostics became more streamlined, reducing unnecessary blood draws, lowering costs, and minimizing follow-up testing caused by inconclusive CK-MB results


By unbundling CK-MB tests from the standard emergency department cardiac panel, the health system streamlined its diagnostics to primarily rely on the more accurate troponin biomarker.


## Understanding the real cost of testing


Discussions about laboratory utilization often focus on the cost of the assay itself. The broader economics extend far beyond the price of a test. Labs and health plans must account for the operational infrastructure required to perform testing and manage reimbursement.


Those operational costs can be significant. Prior authorization management, claims appeals, customer service inquiries, provider education, reimbursement support, data exchange, reporting workflows, and ongoing communication regarding coverage and medical necessity all require resources that contribute to the overall economics of testing.


Patients feel the impact too. When testing pathways are unclear, documentation is incomplete, or members are directed toward out-of-network providers or poorly integrated testing solutions they may experience unexpected bills, delays in care, or confusion about coverage responsibilities.


Financial fairness includes not only appropriate reimbursement between payers and laboratories, but also minimizing avoidable financial hardships for members.


For health plans, these operational and member-facing considerations increasingly influence payer decision-making. The question is no longer simply whether a test carries an acceptable unit cost.


**Payers must evaluate whether a testing partner can support:**


- Efficient ordering
- Clean data exchange
- Consistent reporting
- Transparent billing and coding practices
- A more predictable member experience


A lower-cost testing option may ultimately generate higher administrative costs if it creates additional appeals, customer service volume, manual review requirements, or provider abrasion.


A stewardship-based approach evaluates testing through a comprehensive operational lens. The key question isn't the direct cost of an assay, but whether the overall testing model creates sustainable value while supporting quality care, administrative efficiency, and a positive member experience.


Greater transparency around operational requirements helps health plans assess the impact of various testing programs. It also helps explain why stewardship has become an important strategic consideration in network management and reimbursement policy.


The real cost of testing includes not only what is paid for the assay, but also the downstream effects on providers, plan operations, laboratories, and the patients receiving care.


## Test waste signals a lab stewardship opportunity


Payers frequently view unnecessary testing as a marker of broader inefficiencies. For that reason, modern stewardship programs increasingly focus on identifying low-value, obsolete, duplicative, or clinically outdated testing practices.


Labcorp's stewardship reporting programs, including[Labcorp Insight Analytics and ®](https://www.labcorp.com/data/insight-analytics)[Visiun-based utilization](https://www.visiun.com/) reporting capabilities, help organizations identify testing patterns that may warrant review. Analytics can reveal:


- Duplicate ordering
- Outdated test utilization
- Variation from clinical guidelines
- Opportunities to improve consistency across provider organizations


Organizations that actively evaluate and refine their test menus demonstrate a stronger commitment to[value-based care](https://www.labcorp.com/organizations/organizations-we-serve/value-based) . For payers, that builds credibility because it shows laboratories are actively managing waste rather than simply generating volume.


## In-network status is about more than price


Network strategy plays an important role in lab stewardship. While reimbursement rates remain important, payers often evaluate lab partners through a much broader lens that includes:


- **Access**
- **Transparency**
- **Operational performance**
- **Data quality**
- **Member experience**


Consider "snowbirds,” members who spend portions of the year in different regions who may encounter fragmented testing experiences when they move outside established provider networks. Out-of-network testing can create confusion, administrative complexity, and unexpected financial obligations. These challenges make it difficult to optimize utilization, assess quality, or understand the full member experience.


Large, integrated lab networks can help reduce these challenges by:


- Improving data visibility for patients and providers
- Creating greater consistency across testing workflows
- Supporting more predictable member experiences


Labcorp's stewardship approach aligns testing practices with payer priorities through utilization analytics, consistent testing workflows, clinical decision support resources, and nationwide accessibility.


These capabilities help support both network strategy and clinical quality objectives while creating a more cohesive testing experience across the care continuum.


## How Labcorp supports lab stewardship
